title: Maritime NDT Consulting & Class Audit Support, Panama City
description: Level III audit prep for Panama City yards and NDT firms: naval unit records, stop-work handovers, rehired techs, UR Z17 gauging. Send your review date.
h1: Maritime NDT Consulting and Class Audit Support in Panama City, Florida
html:
Panama City's shipbuilding has spent the last few years building cutters for one federal customer and destroyer sections for another, while also turning out tugs and dredges. Each of those programs leaves a trail of NDT records that someone will audit. This page is for quality managers at Panhandle yards, the NDT subcontractors and gauging firms that work for them, and suppliers feeding naval units to other yards. Atlantis NDT gives ASNT NDT Level III consulting support to get those records and procedures audit-ready; send us the program and the review date to begin.

Panama City's yards and what they build

The local shipbuilding base is dominated by Eastern Shipbuilding Group, which operates three shipyards on Florida's Gulf Coast and describes itself as the largest private-sector employer in Northwest Florida. Its portfolio runs to tugboats, commercial vessels and government work, including the Army Corps of Engineers' Medium Class Hopper Dredge and the Coast Guard's Heritage-class Offshore Patrol Cutter. The lead cutter, Argus (WMSM-915), was christened in Panama City in October 2023.

The cutter program has been difficult. In 2025 the company told the government it could not complete all four cutters on contract without an unabsorbable loss, the Coast Guard stopped work on hulls three and four, and in July 2025 the Department of Homeland Security partially terminated the contract for two of the four. In November 2025 Eastern announced it was suspending work on the program and reducing its workforce, and the government was reported to be considering moving two hulls to another yard. Later production of the class had already been awarded to a different builder in 2022. Program status changes quickly; treat these as the facts reported in 2025, not as the current position.

Alongside the cutters, Eastern has been building outfitted structural units for Flight III Arleigh Burke destroyers under an agreement with HII's Ingalls Shipbuilding announced in September 2025. A grand block for DDG 135, built and inspected at Eastern's Nelson Street facility in Panama City, went by barge to Ingalls in August 2025. Around the main yard sit the usual marine trades: fabricators, outfitting and machining suppliers, repair contractors and inspection firms.

Building destroyer units for a yard in another state

Unit construction moves part of a warship's structure to a supplier, then ships it to the prime for joining. For NDT this creates a problem that ordinary shipbuilding does not have: the examination record for a single hull is now split between two companies, two quality systems and possibly two NDT programs, and the Navy will eventually expect it to read as one.

The prime's purchase order carries the Navy requirements down to the unit builder, including the NAVSEA documents that govern NDT methods, personnel qualification and acceptance. The unit builder's job is to examine every weld it is responsible for, to the extent and method the drawings and specifications require, and to deliver records the prime can merge without rework. In our experience the points that cause friction at the receiving yard are predictable:

  • Weld identification. If the supplier numbers welds its own way, the prime's inspectors cannot match the reports to their drawings. Agree the identification scheme before the first weld.
  • Boundary welds. Erection joints made at the prime are examined there, but welds near unit edges may be examined twice, once before shipping and again after joining heat has been applied nearby. Settle who examines what, and when, in writing.
  • Personnel qualification evidence. The prime and the Navy can ask for the certification files of the supplier's technicians. Those files must satisfy the scheme the contract names, not the supplier's commercial program.
  • Open items at shipment. Repairs not yet re-examined, or examinations deferred because of access, must travel with the unit as a clear list, not be discovered on arrival.
  • Transport damage. A barge move can mark or distort structure. A short pre- and post-shipment visual record protects both sides.

Our pages on the NAVSEA written practice, NAVSEA ultrasonic requirements and NAVSEA NDT requirements for shipyards cover the governing documents. For the receiving end, see maritime NDT consulting in Pascagoula, where Ingalls is based.

When a program stops: keeping NDT records usable

Stop-work orders, terminations and transfers of partly built hulls are rare in most industries and have happened here. They matter for NDT because a hull that may be finished elsewhere will be judged on the records left behind. The next builder, the government's technical staff and eventually the classification or certifying authority will all ask the same questions: which welds were examined, by whom, with what procedure, against what acceptance standard, and what is still open.

A yard facing a stop or a transfer can protect itself and its customer with a few steps:

  1. Freeze and index the records. Make a complete index of NDT reports, data files, technique sheets and weld maps for each affected hull, with the procedure revision that applied to each report.
  2. List open and rejected welds. Every rejected indication should show its repair and re-examination status. Anything unresolved goes on a handover list.
  3. Capture personnel evidence now. When staff reductions follow, the people who signed the reports leave. Make sure their certification files, vision records and examination evidence are retained before they go.
  4. Preserve raw data. Where ultrasonic data were recorded electronically, keep the native files and the software needed to read them, not only the printed summaries.
  5. Record the condition at stoppage. Note any areas left exposed, unpainted or unprotected, because corrosion or damage during a long stop may need re-examination later.

This is the same discipline any audit rewards, applied under pressure. Our guide to NDT audit documentation and the audit evidence scramble page describe how to keep records in a state that survives a handover.

Technicians after a workforce reduction

Layoffs scatter a yard's NDT people across the Gulf Coast. When they are hired back, or hired by a subcontractor that picks up the work, their certification does not simply resume. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A an employer certifies its own staff under its own written practice, and a certification lapses when employment ends. The rehiring company must certify again, using whatever documented training, experience and examination results its written practice allows it to credit. Some programs also treat a long gap in method activity as interrupted service that calls for re-examination before the person signs reports again.

Navy-contract work adds the qualification rules in the governing NAVSEA publication, which have their own treatment of lapses. Keep the two separate, and keep copies of what you relied on when you recertify someone. A practical habit helps here: when someone leaves, add a dated note to their file listing their last certifications, last vision check and the reports they signed in the final month. If they come back, the recertification decision starts from facts rather than memory. Our pages on experience logs and vision examination records cover the files auditors open first.

Tugs, dredges and commercial hulls

Commercial work at Panhandle yards follows a different chain. A classed tug or commercial vessel is built under its classification society's rules, the yard's NDT plan for hull welds is reviewed and accepted by the surveyor, and the yard's NDT personnel and procedures must satisfy the society. Government-owned commercial-type vessels, such as a dredge built for the Army Corps, follow the owner's specification, which may in turn call for class rules or specific codes. Either way the specification sets the examination extent, and the yard's quality manager should be able to point to the clause behind every line of the NDT plan.

Dredges bring wear and erosion into the picture as well as weld quality. Pump casings, suction and discharge piping, hopper structure and dragarms see abrasion that later in service makes thickness surveys a routine maintenance tool. Building a vessel with recorded baseline thicknesses at the locations the owner will monitor saves argument for years afterwards, and is worth proposing even when the specification does not demand it.

Atlantis performs no radiography in the US; exposure work needs a source license under 10 CFR Part 34 and the Florida rules that implement it, so licensed contractors carry it out. Where a specification calls for RT, our Level III can review the contractor's procedure and the images. Where ultrasonic examination is accepted in its place, the technique and its demonstration become central, and our page on procedure qualification and demonstration explains how that is usually proven.

Gauging firms in the Panhandle and class approval

Thickness measurement firms that serve vessels drydocked or repaired along this stretch of coast need UR Z17 approval from a vessel's classification society whenever their readings support a class survey. The approval is specific to the society, so a firm must decide which societies' fleets it will serve. The audit looks at the documented quality system, operator training and supervision, personnel records, equipment and calibration records, written work procedures and control of any subcontracting, and the firm must give a practical demonstration of gauging before approval is granted. For gauging firms the approval comes up for renewal at least every three years, sooner than for most other supplier types.

The practical demonstration is where small firms most often stumble. The auditor wants to see the operator set up and verify the gauge, handle coated surfaces in line with the procedure, take readings at identified locations, record them in the approved report format and spot an implausible value. Rehearsing exactly that, on representative plate, is time well spent. Our service supplier approval guide, the DNV service supplier written practice page and UR Z17 requirements for MT go into more detail, and UTM operator qualification covers the people.

Where Atlantis stands

No classification society has audited Atlantis yet. Its UR Z17 applications to ABS, Lloyd's Register and DNV are under way, and until one of them issues a certificate Atlantis holds no class approval for any service. The company's management system is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001; it holds no inspection-body or laboratory accreditation under ISO/IEC 17020 or 17025. Atlantis is not the Navy's, the Coast Guard's or a prime's auditor and is not a classification society. Your company owns its quality system and certifies its own personnel, and each reviewer decides for itself; we help make the evidence complete.

How an engagement runs for a Panama City client

Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad, none in Florida. We do most document work remotely and plan visits to the Panhandle around the dates that matter.

  • First conversation. Which program and which reviewer: a prime's supplier audit, a government technical review, a class survey or approval audit, or a records handover.
  • Remote review. Written practice, procedures, technique sheets, NDT plans, personnel files and calibration register, marked against the governing documents.
  • Drafting. We write the changes; the person who signs your program documents approves and issues them.
  • Site visit. Record sampling against hulls or units in work, observation of examinations, equipment checks and a mock audit with your team.
  • Close-out. Help writing corrective actions with root cause and objective evidence after the real review.

What to send us

  • The audit or review notice, or the contract and specification clauses covering NDT.
  • For unit work: the prime's purchase order requirements and the weld identification scheme agreed with the prime.
  • Your written practice, procedures and technique sheets with revision status.
  • An NDT plan and its reports for one hull or unit.
  • Personnel files for the technicians who will be sampled, including any rehired after a gap.
  • For gauging firms: the society's application checklist and two recent reports.

Readiness checklist for Panhandle yards and NDT firms

  • A weld identification scheme agreed with every receiving yard before unit work starts.
  • A written split of boundary-weld examinations between supplier and prime.
  • An indexed, retained record set for any hull affected by a stop or transfer.
  • Certification files kept for technicians who have left, and fresh certification for anyone rehired.
  • NDT plans that cite the clause behind each examination.
  • Baseline thickness records proposed for wear-prone dredge components.
  • Procedures under revision control; see the procedures app for one way to manage it.

faq.q: We build structural units for another shipyard. Whose NDT rules apply?
faq.a: The prime's purchase order decides, and on Navy work it flows down the NAVSEA documents the prime's contract invokes. Your program must meet those, not just your commercial practice. See NAVSEA NDT requirements.

faq.q: Who examines the welds at the edge of a unit, us or the receiving yard?
faq.a: Whatever you agree in writing. Erection joints are normally examined where they are welded, but welds near unit boundaries may need re-examination after joining. Leaving it unstated is what causes disputes.

faq.q: Our cutter work was stopped. What NDT records should we keep?
faq.a: All of them, indexed by hull: reports, native data files, technique sheets, weld maps, repair and re-examination records, and the certification files of everyone who signed. A next builder or government reviewer will need them.

faq.q: Do rehired technicians keep their previous certifications?
faq.a: Not automatically under SNT-TC-1A. Certification ends with employment, so the rehiring employer certifies again under its written practice, crediting documented history where the practice allows.

faq.q: Does a gauging firm need class approval for every vessel it measures?
faq.a: Only where the readings support a class survey, and then it needs approval from that vessel's own society. Owner-only checks fall outside UR Z17, though many owners still prefer approved firms.

faq.q: Has Atlantis been approved by a classification society?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has UR Z17 applications with ABS, Lloyd's Register and DNV and has not yet been audited by any of them. It holds no class approval.

faq.q: Will Atlantis take radiography work at a Panama City yard?
faq.a: No. RT in the US needs a source license, so licensed contractors perform it. Atlantis can review the RT procedure and the images as a Level III.

faq.q: Can Atlantis act as our outside Level III?
faq.a: For commercial programs under SNT-TC-1A or CP-189, yes, in ultrasonic, magnetic particle, penetrant, visual and radiographic testing. For Navy work, first confirm what the governing NAVSEA publication requires of the Level III. More on Level III consulting.

faq.q: Can you prepare our welding procedures for unit construction?
faq.a: No. Welding procedures and their qualification belong to your welding engineering staff; Atlantis works on NDT. The WPS, PQR and WPQ explainer shows where the two meet.
Tell us the program, the reviewer and the date through the contact form, and attach your written practice if it is ready to share. Atlantis replies within one business day.
